question: to the Commission Lefteris Nikolaou-Alavanos (NI) Subject:

‘Tourism development’ and the ‘economic miracle’ of the tourism sector are based on the profound exploitation of workers through low wages, intensification of work, exhausting hours, insufficient rest time and the erosion of any labour and insurance rights that remain, with reduced protection for the seasonally unemployed, the writing off of specialisms – such as cooks, maids and pot washers – other than the heavy-duty and unsanitary ones, and the shrinkage of gains such as lump sum payments for hotel employees. An example is the local sectoral collective agreement signed by the Hotel Employees Union and the Rhodes Labour Centre with catering employers, by which they are forcing workers – through a ‘solemn declaration’ that they themselves will sign – to work seven days. Accordingly: 1.

What is the Commission’s position on the fact that while it constantly invokes ‘budgetary restrictions’ with regard to meeting workers’ basic needs, such as supporting the seasonally unemployed, restoring labour and insurance rights and strengthening health and safety measures in the workplace, at the same time it promotes the provocative subsidisation of business groups in the sector and the launch of military spending, allocating billions for armaments programmes in the context of the EU’s war preparations and NATO commitments?

What is the Commission’s position on the promotion and implementation of anti-labour legislation through EU guidelines and directives (2022/2041, 2019/1152, 2019/1158, 2003/88/EC), which have been incorporated into national law over time by all governments and by Nea Dimokratia, leading to further weakening of collective bargaining agreements, the expansion of flexibility with inhumane, exhausting working hours and wage compression?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.9.2026) The Commission does not set national wage levels, unemployment benefits or defence budgets. Under the Treaties, these are primarily matters for Member States, while EU social legislation establishes minimum standards and supports social dialogue. The Commission rejects any abuse of workers’ rights. EU law requires Member States to ensure minimum protection on working time1, transparent and predictable working conditions2, work-life balance3, and adequate minimum wage frameworks4, in line with Directive 2003/88/EC, Directive (EU) 2019/1152, Directive (EU) 2019/1158 and Directive (EU) 2022/2041. These instruments are intended to improve workers’ protection, not reduce it. Their application and enforcement, including in tourism and seasonal work, are the responsibility of national authorities, courts and labour inspectorates. Collective agreements must comply with applicable national and EU law. Any national measures or agreements must respect EU rules on daily and weekly rest, maximum working time and fair working conditions. Regarding funding priorities, EU support for tourism or defence is grounded in distinct legal bases and serves different policy objectives decided by the co-legislators. The Commission encourages Member States to use available EU instruments, including the European Social Fund Plus, to support employment, education and skills, and healthy and well-adapted working environments that address health risks, including for seasonal workers.
1 Directive 2003/88/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 November 2003 concerning certain

aspects of the organisation of working time, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2003/88/oj. 2 Directive (EU) 2019/1152 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on transparent and predictable working conditions, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1152/oj. 3 Directive (EU) 2019/1158 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019 on work-life balance for parents and carers and repealing Council Directive 2010/18/EU, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/1158/oj. 4 Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2022/2041/oj.
